title: What happened?
mission: The frame everything else hangs on: asking what happened, following the answer, and reacting like a native listener. Everyday Arabic — but at real speed, about real things.
sources: Forms cross-checked against Madrasa dictionary and Living Arabic Project (Levantine)
Urban Palestinian koine (Jerusalem/Ramallah); native-speaker review pending — low-confidence items avoided

lessons.title: What happened today?
lessons.canDo: I can ask what happened, follow the basic answer, and ask the follow-up questions — who, when, why.

blocks.body: Every conversation about news — from street gossip to war reporting — runs on one tiny verb: صار, 'it happened.' This lesson installs the question battery you'll use for the rest of the trajectory.

example.en: What happened today?

items.note: Double duty: events happen (صار إشي) and things become (صار غالي — it got expensive).

cognate.note: Same Semitic root, same meaning. A freebie — you already own this verb.

example.en: Did you hear what happened?
Did you see the news yesterday?

items.note: MSA رأى is almost never said on the street — it's شاف everywhere in the Levant.

cognate.note: Sounds like Hebrew חיכה 'waited' — unrelated. حكى is talking, not waiting.

example.en: He talked to me about the situation.

cognate.note: Looks like חבר 'friend' — different root entirely. خبر is news; plural أخبار.

example.en: There's an important piece of news today.

items.note: شو أخبارك؟ — literally 'what's your news?' — is just 'how are you?'

example.en: Seriously? Unbelievable!

items.note: From عن جد — 'in earnest.' The all-purpose 'wait, really?'

cognate.note: Israeli slang borrowed it wholesale. You already use this word — now meet it at home.

example.en: I swear I didn't hear anything.
Nothing happened, calm down.

items.note: Palestinian shibboleth — Lebanese say شي, Egyptians حاجة. From MSA شيء.

cognate.note: Root ḥ-r-m — the sacred/forbidden zone. Hebrew kept the ban (חרם); Arabic حرام 'forbidden' softened into an exclamation of pity.

example.en: What a pity — they lost their house.
Why is it like this? / Why so?

items.note: هيك الوضع — 'that's how things are.' You'll hear it forty times a day.

blocks.title: Did you hear?
blocks.situation: Samer runs into Layla on the street. Something happened downtown this morning.

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: أهلين سامر! الحمدلله. اسمع، سمعت شو صار اليوم؟
lines.en: Hey Samer! Fine, thank God. Listen — did you hear what happened today?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: في مظاهرة كبيرة في وسط البلد، الناس كلها نزلت عالشارع.
lines.en: There's a big demonstration downtown — everyone took to the street.

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: بسبب الأسعار. كل إشي صار غالي.
lines.en: Because of the prices. Everything's gotten expensive.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.en: That's true, wallah. And when was the demonstration?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: شباب، كبار، عيلات كاملة... كل الناس.
lines.en: Young people, old people, whole families... everyone.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.ar: هيك الوضع صعب عالكل. بدي أشوف الأخبار المسا.
lines.en: Yeah — things are hard for everyone. I'll watch the news tonight.

questions.why: ليلى: في مظاهرة كبيرة في وسط البلد.

questions.prompt: Why did people take to the street?
questions.why: كل إشي صار غالي — everything got expensive.
شباب، كبار، عيلات كاملة — كل الناس.

points.explanation: Past-tense endings are your ear's anchors: -it (I/you m.), -ti (you f.), -u (they). They fly by in speech — train on them now and half of every story unlocks.

examples.en: We heard a loud sound this morning.
People heard the news and went out.

points.explanation: صار before a noun or adjective means 'became': the price-protest sentence كل إشي صار غالي is the pattern. Before an event, it means 'happened'. Context decides — and context comes by ear.

items.en: I didn't hear anything about the demonstration.
You seriously didn't hear the news? Really?

items.story: s-m-ʕ / ש-מ-ע. Identical root, identical meaning. اسمع = שמע! — the app's name is an imperative you already understand.

One ancient root, ḥ-r-m, 'set apart — sacred or forbidden.' Hebrew went to the ban and boycott; Arabic went to حرام 'forbidden,' which softened into 'what a pity.' When you later meet مقاطعة 'boycott,' remember the Hebrew cousin sat here all along.
حكى 'he spoke' sounds like חיכה 'he waited.' If you hear حكى معي and think 'waited for me,' the whole story changes. Different roots — just an acoustic trap.

lessons.title: Where the news comes from
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone describing how they get their news, and name the channels, sites, and people involved.

blocks.body: Before the news itself: the words for who carries it. Channels, sites, journalists, correspondents — and the crucial Palestinian distinction between خبر and إشاعة, news and rumor.

example.en: What channel is the news on?

items.note: Also a Telegram/YouTube channel — same word carries old and new media.

example.en: I read the news on a Palestinian site.

items.note: Double duty in news language: a website — and a physical site (موقع القصف, the site of the strike).

example.en: My father reads the paper every morning.
The journalist did an interview with the family.
Al Jazeera's correspondent reported from Gaza.

items.note: Root ر-س-ل 'send' — the one who is sent. Compare رسالة, a message.

example.en: That's not news — that's a rumor.

items.note: Semantic twin of שמועה but a different root: ش-ي-ع is 'to spread.' A rumor is a spread-thing in Arabic, a heard-thing in Hebrew.

cognate.note: Root ṣ-d-q, truth. Arabic: صدّق believe, صديق friend (the true one), صادق honest. Hebrew took it to justice — צדק, צדיק.

example.en: I don't believe everything I hear.

cognate.note: k-ḏ-b = כ-ז-ב, same root, same meaning. Hebrew אַכְזָבָה 'disappointment' is family too — a hope that lied.

example.en: That talk is all lies.
I follow the news on my phone.
The news turned out to be true.

items.note: Sentence-initial صحيح، ... means 'by the way' — صحيح، سمعت شو صار؟

blocks.title: How Umm Mohammad follows the news
blocks.brief: One speaker, natural pace. Listen twice before opening the transcript. A woman describes her morning news routine — and her daughter's media literacy lecture.
preQuestions: How many different news sources does she mention?
Who in the family prefers the newspaper?
What does her daughter warn her about?

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: أنا بصحى الصبح، أول إشي بفتح التلفون.
transcript.en: I wake up in the morning — first thing, I open the phone.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: بشوف تلغرام، في قنوات أخبار فلسطينية كتير.
transcript.en: I check Telegram — there are lots of Palestinian news channels.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: بعدين بسمع الراديو وأنا بعمل القهوة.
transcript.en: Then I listen to the radio while I make the coffee.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: جوزي بحب الجريدة، بس أنا بقول الجريدة بطيئة.
transcript.en: My husband loves the newspaper, but I say the paper is slow.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: كل إشي بصير، بنشوفه عالتلفون أول بأول.
transcript.en: Everything that happens, we see it on the phone as it happens.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: بنتي بتقولّي: يما، مش كل إشي عالفيسبوك صحيح!
transcript.en: My daughter tells me: Mom, not everything on Facebook is true!

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: ومعها حق، في إشاعات كتير هالأيام.
transcript.en: And she's right — there are a lot of rumors these days.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: عشان هيك بتابع صحفيين بعرفهم، مش أي حدا.
transcript.en: That's why I follow journalists I know — not just anyone.

questions.prompt: What does she open first in the morning?
What's her complaint about the newspaper?
questions.why: الجريدة بطيئة — by the time it prints, the phone already told her.

questions.prompt: Why does she follow specific journalists?

blocks.title: The b- prefix: how habits sound

points.explanation: بصحى، بفتح، بشوف، بسمع، بتابع — the b- prefix marks the habitual present. It's the sound of someone describing their routine. Strip it (أصحى، أفتح) and you have the bare form used after بدّي and لازم.

examples.en: I follow the news every day.
I want to follow new journalists. (no b- after بدي)

items.story: Straight match: k-ḏ-b / כ-ז-ב. And Hebrew hides a poem in the family: אַכְזָבָה, disappointment — what a lie leaves behind.
ṣ-d-q split beautifully: Arabic kept truth personal (صدّق believe, صديق the true friend), Hebrew made it institutional (צדק justice, צדיק the righteous). One root, two moral vocabularies.

lessons.title: Reacting like a native
lessons.canDo: I can catch the reactions in a conversation — surprise, sympathy, worry, hope — in real time, and produce the right one myself.

blocks.body: Half of any Palestinian conversation is the listener reacting: عنجد؟ والله؟ يا حرام... These discourse markers are small, constant, and carry the emotional plot. Learn them and suddenly conversations have a shape.

example.en: Unbelievable what happened today!

items.note: From عقل, mind — 'it doesn't fit in the mind.' Works for horror and for delight.

example.en: Of course I heard — the whole town heard.
Are you sure the news is true?

items.note: Statement and question in one word — tone does the work. أكيد. / أكيد؟

cognate.note: Borrowed into Israeli slang as-is. From ما عليه شي — 'nothing's on it.'

example.en: Never mind — not a problem.

items.en: God protect us (worry about what's coming)

example.en: God protect us from what's coming.

items.note: Exact functional twin of השם ישמור. The worry-formula before news you don't want.

cognate.note: Another full borrowing into Hebrew slang. Covers everything from sincere prayer to polite 'probably never.'

example.ar: إن شاء الله بترجع الكهربا قبل المسا.
example.en: Hopefully the electricity comes back before evening.
If only the situation would change.

items.note: The exact functional twin of הלוואי — wistful, frequent, essential.

example.ar: يا سلام، هاد كل إشي عندهم؟
example.en: Oh wow, that's all they've got?

items.note: Flat tone = sarcasm. You'll need this for Arc 4's political commentary.

example.en: How's the family? — Thank God, all fine.

items.note: Functional twin of ברוך השם — including the resigned shrug version.

example.en: What did you hear? — Nothing at all.

blocks.title: The electricity's out
blocks.situation: Abu Yousef comes home with bad news about the neighborhood. Count the reactions — they carry the whole conversation.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.en: Did you hear? They cut the electricity to the whole neighborhood.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: عنجد؟ يا زلمة لسا حاطّين اللحمة بالفريزر!
lines.en: Seriously? Man, we just put the meat in the freezer!

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.en: Never mind — maybe an hour and it's back.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: يا ريت... المرة الماضية ضلّت مقطوعة يومين.
lines.en: If only... last time it stayed out for two days.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: إن شاء الله بترجع قبل المسا.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: أكيد بترجع. مش معقول يومين كمان.
lines.en: It'll be back for sure. No way it's two days again.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.en: Thank God the weather isn't hot.

questions.prompt: A friend sighs «الله يستر» after reading a headline. What are they expressing?

options: A wish that probably won't happen

questions.prompt: Your plans fall through and you tell a Palestinian friend. The natural response:
questions.why: معلش is the consolation move — 'never mind, it's OK.'

questions.prompt: «يا سلام» said in a flat, dry tone means…
questions.why: Tone flips it. The ironic version dominates political talk.

items.ar: والله / معلش / إن شاء الله / أهلين
items.story: Israeli Hebrew borrowed its entire casual-reaction layer from Palestinian Arabic. You've been speaking fragments of this dialect for years — the app just turns the direction around.
Not loans but parallel engineering: two religious cultures built the same emotional valves — the worry-formula and the gratitude-shrug — from the same Semitic toolbox.

lessons.title: Where and when?
lessons.canDo: I can place an event — neighborhood, town, square — and its time, caught by ear.

lessons.title: Who said?
lessons.canDo: I can track who a piece of information came from, and how sure the speaker sounds about it.

lessons.title: Review & free listening
lessons.canDo: I can follow a real 90-second street clip about a local event, unsimplified.
